how: The project starter proposes the community mark after a neighbouring work is completed and a volunteer joins that proposal.
A direct call for more workers recruits hands for the shared mark.
A volunteer briefly commits to help while calling the design easy enough.
The proposal receives an explicit written acceptance, supporting the visible joining branch without showing how silent readers answered.
A project proposal precedes a later recruitment call without an explicit statement that the starter caused that call.
The causal mechanism connecting the starter to the later recruitment call remains unobserved although their order is visible.
Recruitment and later progress are documented without identifying participants as arriving because of the particular call.
Requests for workers and repairs establish demand for help but do not establish a judgement that the community cannot hold its work.
Members negotiate design size, alternative artwork, fidelity to the original logo, and avoiding mutually destructive revisions.
An answered location question makes the work findable through neighbouring landmarks at the locating end of the element's range.
Members report another logo taking shape below the first creation rather than treating banner completion as the end of construction.
An explicit completion update names cleanup and defence as the next work.
The transition applies to completed parts while further logo construction and design revision can continue alongside upkeep.
One member multiplies placements with old accounts in separate browsers to accelerate work.
Spare-account use establishes acceleration but supports a defence-pressure mechanism only if that motive is evidenced separately.
An improvised initial design neither tests the cross-room frequency claim nor establishes that unseen planning lacked decided order.
A developing logo and continuing design disagreement do not establish that posting a template settled the agreed design.
Members watch both murals, repair vandalism, raise alarms, and request help with damaged edges.
Contributing to a new adjoining work depends on spare attention after defending an existing neighbour, reversing a simple build-then-defend order.
A suspicion about obstructive throwaway accounts receives an explicit identification as attempted help and an offer to stop.
Participants spare neighbouring images, stop overlap, invoke a no-erasing norm, and yield desired space.
Boundary accommodation takes the limited forms of letting a neighbouring tongue cross the border and yielding requested space.
A warning about retaliation makes restoring a damaged neighbour a pragmatic way to protect the community's own mural.
Restraint need not follow a negotiated border because a no-erasing norm and anticipated retaliation supply explicit independent reasons.
Anger about a forced border establishes a clash without showing negotiation caused by the preceding upkeep.
A neighbour's complaint of complete overwriting receives an apology and offers of pixels for nearby reconstruction.
A damage complaint can trigger apology and reconstruction offers without a preceding evidenced call to attack.
Participants contribute across adjoining communities, report defending neighbours, and request help for the neighbouring mural under assault.
Mutual assistance is visible without evidence that shortage caused a request which produced the reported assistance.
Offers to rebuild follow a damage complaint rather than an evidenced border bargain exchanging room for upkeep.
Shared watching and assistance do not independently establish a coalition-forming agreement or shared governing hub.
Defending neighbouring works does not identify a transition from upkeep into joining a coalition.
A member relays another builder's request to move one pixel, enacting a minimal envoy role without evidenced appointment.
Locating adjoining marks and sharing defence do not establish a host's authority over a guest work.
An individual reports yielding requested space without a cited dispute over who can bind the community.
The reported accommodation does not show agreement producing a dispute over representative authority.
Late repairs and a favourable ending report leave relocation after losing the mark unobserved rather than historically ruled out.
The record does not establish either the capacity judgement or relocation needed to test the proposed loss-and-move mechanism.
The senpai-and-kouhai analogy casts shared protection in familiar fandom relationships without establishing ideological mobilisation.
Fandom language and concern for recognisable artwork do not establish a quarrel carried in from before the canvas.
A protective fandom analogy does not identify a prior rivalry naming a target in an attack turn.
The cited project and recruitment concepts do not establish a host-sub April Fools licence making the call a possible joke.
Recruitment and collective praise leave moderation or member boundary-setting around canvas talk unobserved.
Calls are evidenced but no cited response shows a canvas flood producing host boundary-setting.
Members celebrate the adjoining finished murals and credit designers, builders, and defenders as a team.
A speaker explicitly celebrates both represented works and commits to watching and repairing them.
Members share whole-canvas development and an enlarged local timelapse, with explicit thanks for the latter.
The speaker who declares the project ended immediately supplies a timelapse of its development as a reply to that declaration.
A brief thanks acknowledges the enlarged timelapse without asking for another action.
Retrospective comments retain an improvised start, destruction and re-formation, and competing memories of a name and checkerboard struggle.
Fear of damaging a valued shared work can keep an admiring observer from contributing even when the completed work receives enthusiastic praise.
A wish for another canvas receives speculation about next April, meeting the minimal continuation range rather than merely marking this ending.
A future-canvas hope occurs within retrospective discussion without attributing that hope to viewing a preserved record.
Remembering a checkerboard battle does not establish a post-close dispute over correcting or preserving a shared version of the canvas.
Participants seek acknowledgement from the people represented by the artwork, extending completion beyond internal credit or preserving a record.
A neighbour reports actual encroachment during construction, establishing damage without proving an intentional raid or attack call.
Recruitment and subsequent overwriting support a call-to-attack inference only when an attack intention or instruction is independently evidenced.
Anger about a forced border supplies a limited live verbal grievance without establishing a two-sided campaign or post-close score-settling.
The live grievance and the neighbour's complaint do not identify an initiating attack call that caused a continuing verbal contest.
Accommodation and repair are visible without an evidenced initiating attack call that prompted a truce or alternative deal.
